parts.answer: 20.0 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the pH changes as the alkali is added.
parts.answer: pH rises slowly at first, then rises very sharply (from about 2.6 to 11.4) close to the neutral point, then rises slowly again.
parts.working: Slow rise at first B1; sudden large rise around 20 cm³ then levelling off B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.10 mol/dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation.
parts.answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the products when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with:
(i) magnesium
(ii) calcium carbonate
(iii) sodium hydroxide
parts.answer: (i) magnesium chloride + hydrogen (ii) calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide (iii) sodium chloride + water

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of a dilute acid on blue litmus paper and on methyl orange.
parts.answer: Blue litmus turns red; methyl orange turns red.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sodium carbonate powder is added to dilute nitric acid. Which gas is given off?
A carbon dioxide
B hydrogen
C nitrogen dioxide
D oxygen
parts.answer: A carbon dioxide
parts.working: Acids react with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Hydrogen is given off when an acid reacts with a metal, not a carbonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write balanced equations for:
(i) zinc reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid
(ii) copper(II) carbonate reacting with dilute sulfuric acid
parts.answer:
(i) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
(ii) CuCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of any acid with any alkali.
parts.answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the ion present in all aqueous alkalis and state the pH range of alkaline solutions.
parts.answer: hydroxide ion, OH⁻; pH above 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solid ammonium sulfate is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. A gas is given off. Name the gas and give a test for it.
parts.answer: ammonia; turns damp red litmus paper blue
parts.working: Name B1; test with result B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: ammonium sulfate + sodium hydroxide → sodium sulfate + ammonia + water

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use this reaction to explain why a farmer should not spread slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) on a field at the same time as an ammonium fertiliser.
parts.answer: The base reacts with the ammonium salt and nitrogen is lost as ammonia gas.

stem:
Rain and decomposing plant matter have made the soil in a field acidic. A farmer neutralises the acidity with calcium hydroxide. Treat the acidity as equivalent to 4.9 kg of sulfuric acid.
Ca(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + 2H₂O
[Ar: H, 1; O, 16; S, 32; Ca, 40]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sulfuric acid in 4.9 kg.
parts.answer: 50 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium hydroxide needed, in kg.
parts.answer: 3.7 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the farmer uses calcium hydroxide instead of sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Calcium hydroxide is cheaper and only slightly soluble, so it is less likely to make the soil too alkaline / it is less corrosive.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An antacid tablet contains 0.29 g of magnesium hydroxide, which neutralises excess stomach acid.
Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O
[Ar: H, 1; O, 16; Mg, 24]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of magnesium hydroxide in one tablet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.10 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid that one tablet can neutralise, in cm³.
parts.answer: 100 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium hydroxide is a base but not an alkali. Explain why.
parts.answer: It is insoluble in water (an alkali is a soluble base).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Oxides: sulfur dioxide, magnesium oxide, aluminium oxide, carbon monoxide, calcium oxide, carbon dioxide

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.
parts.answer: Acidic: sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide. Basic: magnesium oxide, calcium oxide. Amphoteric: aluminium oxide. Neutral: carbon monoxide.
parts.working: All six correct B3; four or five B2; two or three B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the general type of element that forms (i) acidic oxides and (ii) basic oxides.
parts.answer: (i) non-metals (ii) metals

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which oxide reacts with both dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A copper(II) oxide
B sulfur dioxide
C sodium oxide
D zinc oxide
parts.answer: D zinc oxide
parts.working: Zinc oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with both acids and alkalis. Copper(II) oxide is basic and reacts only with acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium oxide is an amphoteric oxide. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: It reacts with both acids and bases (alkalis) to form salts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of aluminium oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a simple experiment to show that aluminium oxide is amphoteric.
parts.answer: Add some aluminium oxide powder to warm dilute hydrochloric acid and some to warm aqueous sodium hydroxide; it dissolves (reacts) in both.
parts.working: Add to an acid and to an alkali B1; dissolves in both B1

stem: A student burns small samples of magnesium, sulfur and carbon separately in jars of oxygen. Water and a few drops of universal indicator are then shaken in each jar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the colour of the indicator in each jar and explain.
parts.answer: Magnesium: blue/purple — magnesium oxide is basic (forms an alkaline solution). Sulfur: red — sulfur dioxide is acidic. Carbon: yellow/orange — carbon dioxide forms a weakly acidic solution.
parts.working: Each correct colour with reason B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the burning of magnesium.
parts.answer: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety precaution when burning sulfur.
parts.answer: Use a fume cupboard (sulfur dioxide is toxic).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four oxides, W, X, Y and Z, are tested.
Oxide | effect of water | reacts with dilute HCl? | reacts with aqueous NaOH?
W | dissolves, pH 13 | yes | no
X | insoluble | yes | yes
Y | dissolves, pH 2 | no | yes
Z | insoluble | no | no

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.
parts.answer: W basic; X amphoteric; Y acidic; Z neutral
parts.working: All four B2; two or three B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a possible identity for each of W, X, Y and Z from: aluminium oxide, carbon monoxide, sodium oxide, sulfur trioxide.
parts.answer: W sodium oxide; X aluminium oxide; Y sulfur trioxide; Z carbon monoxide
parts.working: All four B2; two or three B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of oxide W with water.
parts.answer: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State one source of each pollutant.
(i) carbon monoxide
(ii) sulfur dioxide
(iii) oxides of nitrogen
(iv) methane
parts.answer: (i) incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels (ii) burning fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds (iii) reaction of nitrogen and oxygen in hot car engines (iv) decomposition of vegetation / waste gases from digestion in animals (livestock)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one adverse effect of particulates (soot) in the air.
parts.answer: Increased risk of respiratory problems (and cancer).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A faulty gas heater in a closed room produces a colourless, odourless, toxic gas. What is the gas?
A carbon dioxide
B carbon monoxide
C nitrogen dioxide
D sulfur dioxide
parts.answer: B carbon monoxide
parts.working: Incomplete combustion of the fuel in a shortage of oxygen gives carbon monoxide, which is toxic and has no colour or smell. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide are toxic but have strong smells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sulfur dioxide from a coal-fired power station dissolves in rainwater. Name the environmental problem this causes.
parts.answer: acid rain

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two effects of this problem.
parts.answer: Any two of: damages/corrodes buildings and statues made of limestone or marble; corrodes metal structures; kills fish and other life in lakes; damages trees/plants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing the sulfur dioxide released by power stations.
parts.answer: Remove sulfur from the fuel / use low-sulfur fuel / flue gas desulfurisation (react SO₂ with calcium oxide).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how oxides of nitrogen are formed in a car engine.
parts.answer: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together at the very high temperature inside the engine.
parts.working: Nitrogen and oxygen (from air) react B1; high temperature B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the formation of nitrogen monoxide, NO.
parts.answer: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two adverse effects of oxides of nitrogen.
parts.answer: Acid rain; photochemical smog; respiratory problems.

stem: Modern cars have catalytic converters in their exhaust systems.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete and balance the equation for the removal of carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in a catalytic converter.
__CO + __NO → __CO₂ + __
parts.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂
parts.working: N₂ as product B1; balancing B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the substance that is oxidised in this reaction. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide; it gains oxygen (oxidation number of C increases from +2 to +4).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other type of pollutant removed in the catalytic converter and state what it is converted to.
parts.answer: Unburned hydrocarbons; oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In flue gas desulfurisation, waste gases from a power station pass through calcium oxide. Write the equation for the reaction of calcium oxide with sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the types of oxide, why this reaction happens.
parts.answer: Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and sulfur dioxide is an acidic oxide, so they react (neutralise) to form a salt.
parts.working: CaO basic B1; SO₂ acidic, so neutralisation B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Powdered calcium carbonate can be used instead. Suggest one advantage of using calcium carbonate.
parts.answer: It is cheap and plentiful (limestone), and is safer to handle than calcium oxide.

stem: During winter, Lahore often has thick smog. Measurements show high levels of particulates and oxides of nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two sources of the particulates.
parts.answer: Any two of: diesel vehicle exhausts; burning crop stubble; brick kilns/industry burning coal or waste; burning rubbish.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why smog is harmful to people.
parts.answer: Particulates and NOₓ irritate the lungs and cause or worsen respiratory problems such as asthma.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions that would reduce smog.
parts.answer: Any two of: use catalytic converters; more public transport/electric vehicles; stop crop burning; cleaner kilns/filters on factory chimneys; low-sulfur fuels.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gas in car exhaust is NOT removed by a catalytic converter?
A carbon dioxide
B carbon monoxide
C nitrogen monoxide
D unburned hydrocarbons
parts.answer: A carbon dioxide
parts.working: The converter changes CO, NO and unburned hydrocarbons into CO₂, N₂ and H₂O, so it removes B, C and D but actually produces more carbon dioxide. CO is removed by oxidation to CO₂.

stem:
A brick kiln burns 1000 kg of coal that contains 1.6 % sulfur by mass. All the sulfur is converted to sulfur dioxide: S + O₂ → SO₂
[Ar: O, 16; S, 32; Ca, 40]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur in the coal.
parts.answer: 16 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced.
parts.answer: 32 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium oxide needed to remove all of this sulfur dioxide (CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃).
parts.answer: 28 kg

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An air-quality monitor next to a busy road records the average concentration of carbon monoxide each day for one week.
Day | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun
CO / µg per m³ | 1850 | 1920 | 1780 | 1890 | 2100 | 1150 | 860

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean concentration for Monday to Friday. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 1908 µg per m³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease from Friday to Sunday, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a reason for the lower values at the weekend.
parts.answer: Less traffic (fewer people driving to work/school).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous to health.
parts.answer: It is toxic: it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: When petrol (octane, C₈H₁₈) burns in a limited supply of air, carbon monoxide and water are formed. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: 2C₈H₁₈ + 17O₂ → 16CO + 18H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a car engine running in a closed garage is particularly dangerous.
parts.answer: The oxygen in the garage gets used up, so combustion becomes more incomplete and more carbon monoxide forms; carbon monoxide is toxic and builds up in the closed space.
parts.working: Less oxygen → more incomplete combustion/CO B1; CO toxic and accumulates B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane.
parts.answer: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test for water, giving the result.
parts.answer: Add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: it turns from white to blue. (Or: cobalt(II) chloride paper turns from blue to pink.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a physical test to show that a sample of water is pure.
parts.answer: Measure its boiling point (100 °C) or melting point (0 °C); pure water boils at exactly 100 °C / melts at exactly 0 °C.
parts.working: Measure boiling or melting point B1; correct value B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which stage of drinking-water treatment kills harmful microbes?
A chlorination
B filtration
C sedimentation
D treatment with carbon
parts.answer: A chlorination
parts.working: Chlorine kills bacteria and other microbes. Filtration removes insoluble particles but does not kill microbes.

stem: Water from the Indus is treated before it is supplied to homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each stage:
(i) sedimentation and filtration
(ii) treatment with carbon
(iii) chlorination
parts.answer: (i) remove insoluble solids (ii) remove tastes and odours (iii) kill microbes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Even after treatment, tap water is not pure water. Explain why.
parts.answer: It still contains dissolved substances (salts/minerals and some chlorine).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Water from natural sources contains many substances. Name two substances in river water that are beneficial and explain why.
parts.answer: Dissolved oxygen, which is needed by aquatic life; some mineral salts/metal compounds that provide essential minerals for life.
parts.working: Dissolved oxygen for fish/aquatic life B1; mineral salts as essential minerals B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three substances found in polluted water that are harmful, and give one effect of one of them.
parts.answer: Any three of: some metal compounds (toxic); plastics (harm wildlife); sewage (contains harmful microbes, causes disease); harmful microbes; nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers (deoxygenation, damage to aquatic life). Effect e.g. sewage microbes cause diseases such as cholera.
parts.working: Any three harmful substances B2 (two B1); one correct effect B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Excess nitrate fertiliser washes from farmland into a lake. Describe how this can lead to the death of fish.
parts.answer: Nitrates cause rapid growth of algae (algal bloom) on the surface; algae block light so plants below die; algae and plants die and are decomposed by bacteria; the bacteria use up dissolved oxygen, so fish die (deoxygenation).
parts.working: Algae grow rapidly B1; plants/algae die B1; bacteria decompose them using oxygen B1; less dissolved oxygen so fish die B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one other type of compound from fertilisers or detergents that causes the same problem.
parts.answer: phosphates

stem:
A student evaporates 250 cm³ of a tap-water sample to dryness in a weighed evaporating basin.
Mass of empty basin = 52.316 g
Mass of basin + residue = 52.401 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of dissolved solids in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of dissolved solids in g/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.34 g/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: The sample boils at 100.1 °C. Explain what this, and the residue, show about the water.
parts.answer: It is not pure; dissolved substances raise the boiling point and leave a residue.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a balance reading to 0.001 g is needed.
parts.answer: The mass of residue is very small, so a less precise balance would give a large percentage error.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student compares the dissolved solids in three water samples. She evaporates 100 cm³ of each sample to dryness in a weighed basin.
Sample | mass of empty basin / g | mass of basin + residue / g
river water | 45.210 | 45.262
tube-well water | 44.875 | 44.931
bottled water | 46.020 | 46.035

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of residue from each sample.
parts.answer: river 0.052 g; tube-well 0.056 g; bottled 0.015 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of dissolved solids in the tube-well water in g/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.56 g/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which sample contained the most dissolved solids? State one other test she should do before deciding that this water is unsafe to drink.
parts.answer: Tube-well water; e.g. test for harmful microbes / test for toxic metal compounds or nitrates (dissolved solids are not all harmful).
parts.working: Tube-well B1; sensible further test B1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat each sample and take a mean / use a larger volume of water.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two greenhouse gases.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide and methane

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each gas, state one human activity that increases its amount in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels (or deforestation). Methane: livestock farming (cattle) / rice paddies / landfill waste decomposition.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
A combustion of wood
B photosynthesis
C respiration
D decomposition of dead leaves
parts.answer: B photosynthesis
parts.working: Green plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis to make glucose. Combustion, respiration and decomposition all release carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how greenhouse gases cause the Earth's surface to warm up.
parts.answer: Thermal energy from the Sun warms the Earth's surface, which emits infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb this infrared radiation; they re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth, so less escapes to space and the surface warms.
parts.working: Earth's surface emits infrared/thermal energy B1; greenhouse gases absorb it B1; re-emit it back towards Earth (less escapes to space) B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible effects of climate change.
parts.answer: Any two of: rising sea levels; melting glaciers/ice caps; more frequent floods, droughts or heatwaves; changes in crop yields; loss of habitats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
parts.answer:
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
parts.working: Word equation B1; balanced symbol equation B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two processes in the carbon cycle that return carbon dioxide to the air.
parts.answer: respiration and combustion (also decomposition)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how cutting down large areas of forest affects the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Fewer trees carry out photosynthesis, so less CO₂ is removed (and burning or decay of the trees releases CO₂), so the amount increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three ways a country could reduce its emissions of carbon dioxide and methane.
parts.answer: Any three of: use renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric) instead of fossil fuels; increase use of hydrogen as a fuel; plant trees; reduce livestock farming; reduce waste in landfill; improve public transport/energy efficiency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using electric cars charged from coal-fired power stations does little to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.
parts.answer: The coal burned in the power station still produces carbon dioxide.

stem:
A household uses natural gas (methane) for cooking. In one month it burns 1.6 kg of methane.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
[Ar: H, 1; C, 12; O, 16. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced.
parts.answer: 4.4 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of this carbon dioxide at r.t.p., in dm³.
parts.answer: 2400 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Methane that leaks without burning is also a problem. Explain why.
parts.answer: Methane is a greenhouse gas (stronger than carbon dioxide), so leaks add to global warming.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The table shows the average concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, measured at a remote observatory.
Year | 1960 | 1980 | 2000 | 2020
CO₂ / parts per million (ppm) | 317 | 339 | 370 | 414

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average increase per year between 1960 and 1980, and between 2000 and 2020.
parts.answer: 1.1 ppm per year; 2.2 ppm per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average increase per year over the whole period 1960–2020, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.62 ppm per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend and suggest a reason for it.
parts.answer: The concentration increases, and the rate of increase is getting faster; more fossil fuels are burned (more energy use, vehicles, industry) and more deforestation.
parts.working: Increasing at an increasing rate B1; reason B1

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: NPK fertilisers provide three elements needed for plant growth. Name the three elements.
parts.answer: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one compound used in fertilisers to provide nitrogen.
parts.answer: ammonium nitrate (or ammonium sulfate / ammonium phosphate / potassium nitrate)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why farmers add fertilisers to their fields.
parts.answer: To replace elements removed by crops and improve plant growth / crop yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which fertiliser a farmer should choose to supply the most nitrogen per kilogram.
parts.answer: ammonium nitrate

stem:
A farmer in Sahiwal compares two nitrogen fertilisers. (The prices are invented for this question.)
Fertiliser | formula | mass of bag | price of bag
urea | CO(NH₂)₂ | 50 kg | Rs 4800
ammonium nitrate | NH₄NO₃ | 50 kg | Rs 4200
[Ar: H, 1; C, 12; N, 14; O, 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen in one bag of urea, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of 1 kg of nitrogen from each fertiliser, to the nearest rupee, and state which is better value.
parts.answer: urea Rs 206 per kg N; ammonium nitrate Rs 240 per kg N; urea is better value

parts.label: c
parts.text: The soil is also acidic. Explain why the farmer should not add lime at the same time as ammonium nitrate.
parts.answer: The base reacts with ammonium ions, releasing ammonia gas, so nitrogen is lost.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the approximate percentage by volume of nitrogen in clean, dry air?
A 21 %
B 50 %
C 78 %
D 99 %
parts.working: Clean dry air is about 78 % nitrogen and 21 % oxygen, with small amounts of argon and carbon dioxide. 21 % is the figure for oxygen.

stem:
100 cm³ of dry air is pushed backwards and forwards between two gas syringes over a tube of heated copper powder. The copper turns black. The apparatus is allowed to cool and the volume is measured. This is repeated until the volume stops changing.
Reading | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
Volume of gas / cm³ | 85 | 80 | 79 | 79

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of copper with oxygen.
parts.answer: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the apparatus is cooled before each reading.
parts.answer: Gases expand when hot, so a hot gas would give a volume that is too large.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the main gas left in the syringe and one other gas present in small amounts.
parts.answer: nitrogen; argon (or carbon dioxide)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions and nitrogen forms N³⁻ ions. What is the formula of magnesium nitride?
A Mg₃N₂
B Mg₂N₃
C MgN
D Mg₂N
parts.answer: A Mg₃N₂
parts.working: Charges must balance: 3 × (+2) = +6 and 2 × (−3) = −6, so Mg₃N₂. Mg₂N₃ (B) simply swaps the numbers the wrong way and gives +4 and −9.

stem: Sodium chloride is obtained from rock salt mined at Khewra in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The electronic configuration of a sodium atom is 2,8,1 and of a chlorine atom is 2,8,7. Describe what happens to the electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride.
parts.answer: Each sodium atom transfers (loses) its one outer electron to a chlorine atom, which gains it; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions form.
parts.working: B1 one electron transferred from Na to Cl; B1 Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions formed (both with full outer shells).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of the sodium ion and of the chloride ion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Calcium oxide (quicklime) is made in lime kilns and used in cement and to treat acidic soil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for calcium oxide. Show the outer-shell electrons and the charges on the ions.
parts.answer: Calcium transfers two electrons to oxygen. Ca²⁺ has 8 electrons in its outer shell (2,8,8) and O²⁻ has 8 electrons in its outer shell (2,8), shown as 6 dots + 2 crosses; charges 2+ and 2−.
parts.working: B1 two electrons transferred from Ca to O; B1 both ions shown with 8 outer electrons (O²⁻: 6 of its own + 2 from Ca); B1 charges Ca²⁺ and O²⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium oxide melts at about 2600 °C. Explain why it has such a high melting point.
parts.answer: It is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces.
parts.working: B1 giant lattice / many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions; B1 much energy needed to overcome them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Suggest why calcium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
parts.answer: The ions in calcium oxide have larger charges (2+ and 2−) so the attraction between them is stronger.
parts.working: B1 higher charges on ions → stronger attraction.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use the ions K⁺, Al³⁺, Fe³⁺, O²⁻, OH⁻, NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻ to write the formulae of:
(i) potassium oxide
(ii) aluminium sulfate
(iii) iron(III) hydroxide
(iv) aluminium nitrate
parts.answer: (i) K₂O  (ii) Al₂(SO₄)₃  (iii) Fe(OH)₃  (iv) Al(NO₃)₃
parts.working: B1 each. Brackets are needed around SO₄, OH and NO₃ when there is more than one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solid potassium bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten potassium bromide does. Explain this difference.
parts.answer: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 ions present in both; B1 ions fixed / cannot move in solid; B1 ions mobile in molten (or aqueous) state.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other condition in which potassium bromide conducts electricity.
parts.answer: When dissolved in water (aqueous solution).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lithium (2,1) reacts with nitrogen (2,5) to form the ionic compound lithium nitride, Li₃N. Explain, in terms of electron transfer, why the formula is Li₃N.
parts.answer: Each lithium atom loses one electron to form Li⁺. A nitrogen atom needs to gain three electrons to form N³⁻ (2,8). So three lithium atoms are needed for each nitrogen atom.
parts.working: B1 Li loses 1 e⁻ → Li⁺; B1 N gains 3 e⁻ → N³⁻; B1 three Li needed per N so charges balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of protons and electrons in (i) a lithium ion, Li⁺ (ii) a nitride ion, N³⁻. (Proton numbers: Li = 3, N = 7.)
parts.answer: (i) 3 protons, 2 electrons  (ii) 7 protons, 10 electrons
parts.working: B1 each pair. Electrons = protons − charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An ion X²⁻ contains 18 electrons and 16 neutrons. Deduce the proton number and nucleon (mass) number of X, and identify X.
parts.answer: Proton number 16; nucleon number 32; X is sulfur (the ion is S²⁻).
parts.working: M1 protons = 18 − 2 = 16; A1 nucleon number = 16 + 16 = 32; B1 sulfur.

parts.label: b
parts.text: X forms an ionic compound with aluminium. Write its formula.
parts.answer: Al₂S₃

parts.label: c
parts.text: The ion X²⁻ has the same electronic configuration as an argon atom. Suggest why its chemical properties are different from those of argon.
parts.answer: Both have 2,8,8, but the ion has only 16 protons and a 2− charge; it is attracted to positive ions and can lose electrons (be oxidised), whereas argon is a neutral atom.
parts.working: B1 same configuration 2,8,8; B1 different number of protons / ion is charged, so attracts positive ions or can be oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Which statement about this atom is correct?
A Its nucleon number is 23 and it has 11 electrons.
B Its nucleon number is 12 and it has 11 electrons.
C Its nucleon number is 23 and it has 12 electrons.
D Its proton number is 23 and it has 11 electrons.
parts.answer: A Its nucleon number is 23 and it has 11 electrons.
parts.working: Nucleon number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23; a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons (11). C wrongly uses the neutron number for electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An atom of potassium is shown as ³⁹₁₉K. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom.
parts.answer: 19 protons, 20 neutrons, 19 electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of the potassium atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. State what is meant by the term isotopes.
parts.answer: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
parts.working: B1 same proton number / same element; B1 different number of neutrons (different nucleon number).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both isotopes of chlorine have the same chemical properties.
parts.answer: They have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration (7 outer electrons).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in an atom of chlorine-37. (Proton number of Cl = 17.)

stem: Boron compounds are used to make heat-resistant glassware for laboratories.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Boron has two isotopes: boron-10 (abundance 19.9 %) and boron-11 (abundance 80.1 %). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in each isotope. (Proton number of B = 5.)
parts.answer: boron-10: 5; boron-11: 6

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of magnesium contains 79.0 % magnesium-24, 10.0 % magnesium-25 and 11.0 % magnesium-26. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion ²⁶Mg²⁺. (Proton number of Mg = 12.)
parts.answer: 12 protons, 14 neutrons, 10 electrons
parts.working: B1 neutrons 14; B1 protons 12 and electrons 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gallium has two isotopes, gallium-69 and gallium-71. The relative atomic mass of gallium is 69.72. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
parts.answer: gallium-69: 64 %; gallium-71: 36 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the relative atomic mass of gallium is closer to 69 than to 71.
parts.answer: Gallium-69 is the more abundant isotope.

stem:
Four particles are described below.
W: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 17 electrons
X: 17 protons, 20 neutrons, 17 electrons
Y: 18 protons, 22 neutrons, 18 electrons
Z: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which two particles are isotopes of the same element. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: W and X: both have 17 protons but different numbers of neutrons (18 and 20).
parts.working: B1 W and X; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which particle is a negative ion. Give its symbol with charge.
parts.answer: Z; Cl⁻ (17 protons, 18 electrons)
parts.working: B1 Z; B1 Cl⁻ (one more electron than protons).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the nucleon number of Y and explain why Y is unreactive.
parts.answer: 40; Y is argon with configuration 2,8,8 — a full outer shell, so it does not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
parts.working: B1 18 + 22 = 40; B1 full outer shell / stable configuration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecule contains a triple covalent bond?
A O₂
B N₂
C Cl₂
D CH₄
parts.answer: B N₂
parts.working: N₂ has N≡N (three shared pairs) so each N has 8 outer electrons. O₂ (A) has a double bond, Cl₂ a single bond, CH₄ four single bonds.

stem: Natural gas, which is mainly methane, is piped to many homes for cooking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in a molecule of methane, CH₄. Include the number of shared pairs and the number of outer-shell electrons around each atom.
parts.answer: Carbon shares one pair of electrons with each of four hydrogen atoms: four single covalent bonds (4 shared pairs). Carbon then has 8 outer electrons and each hydrogen has 2.
parts.working: B1 covalent bond = shared pair of electrons; B1 four shared pairs / single bonds; B1 C has 8 and each H has 2 outer electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Methane boils at −162 °C. Explain why its boiling point is so low.
parts.answer: Methane is a simple molecular substance; the intermolecular forces between molecules are weak, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces (not covalent bonds broken); B1 little energy needed.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, the dot-and-cross diagram for a molecule of carbon dioxide, CO₂. Show only outer-shell electrons.
parts.answer: Carbon in the centre forms a double bond (two shared pairs) with each oxygen atom. Each oxygen also has two non-bonding (lone) pairs. Every atom has 8 outer electrons.
parts.working: B1 two double bonds / four shared pairs; B1 two lone pairs on each O; B1 8 electrons around each atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons that are shared in one CO₂ molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methanol has the structural formula CH₃OH. State the number of covalent bonds (bonding pairs) in one molecule and the number of non-bonding pairs on the oxygen atom.
parts.answer: 5 bonding pairs; 2 non-bonding pairs on oxygen
parts.working: B1 5 (three C–H, one C–O, one O–H); B1 2 lone pairs (O has 6 outer electrons, 2 used in bonds).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen chloride is a covalent gas. Explain why pure hydrogen chloride does not conduct electricity.
parts.answer: It is made of neutral molecules; there are no ions or delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 molecules / no ions; B1 no mobile charged particles.

stem:
Melting and boiling points of three halogens:
chlorine, Cl₂: m.p. −101 °C, b.p. −34 °C
bromine, Br₂: m.p. −7 °C, b.p. 59 °C
iodine, I₂: m.p. 114 °C, b.p. 184 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the physical state of each substance at 25 °C.
parts.answer: chlorine: gas; bromine: liquid; iodine: solid
parts.working: 2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the trend in boiling points from chlorine to iodine.
parts.answer: The molecules get larger (more electrons), so the intermolecular forces get stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 larger molecules down the group; B1 stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to overcome.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says 'when bromine boils, the Br–Br bonds break'. Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: Boiling only separates whole Br₂ molecules by overcoming weak intermolecular forces; the strong covalent Br–Br bond inside each molecule stays intact.
parts.working: B1 intermolecular forces overcome; B1 covalent bonds within molecules not broken (Br₂ molecules remain).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure and bonding in a metal such as copper.
parts.answer: A giant lattice of positive metal ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons; the bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
parts.working: B1 lattice of positive ions; B1 delocalised electrons / attraction between ions and electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why copper conducts electricity when solid.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure and carry charge.

stem: Electricians in Faisalabad use copper wire for house wiring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is drawn into thin wires for electrical cables. Explain, in terms of structure, why metals can be bent and drawn into wires without breaking.
parts.answer: The positive ions are arranged in layers. When a force is applied the layers slide over each other. The delocalised electrons move with them, so the metallic bonding is not broken.
parts.working: B1 layers of ions; B1 layers slide over one another; B1 bonding remains because electrons are delocalised (attraction kept in new positions).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium melts at 98 °C and magnesium melts at 650 °C. Both are metals in Period 3. Suggest why magnesium has the higher melting point.
parts.answer: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions and gives two delocalised electrons per atom, while sodium forms Na⁺ and gives one. So the attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger in magnesium and more energy is needed to break it.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ vs Na⁺ (higher charge); B1 more delocalised electrons per atom in Mg; B1 stronger metallic bonding / more energy needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity even though solid sodium does.
parts.answer: Sodium has delocalised electrons that can move; in solid sodium chloride the ions are fixed in the lattice and there are no free electrons.
parts.working: B1 metal: mobile delocalised electrons; B1 ionic solid: ions cannot move.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table gives properties of four substances.
substance: melting point / conducts when solid / conducts when molten
P: 1710 °C / no / no
Q: 801 °C / no / yes
R: −95 °C / no / no
S: 1085 °C / yes / yes
Which substance has a giant ionic structure?
A P
B Q
C R
D S
parts.answer: B Q
parts.working: Q: high melting point, conducts only when molten (ions become mobile). P (A) has a high melting point but never conducts, so it is giant covalent.

stem:
A student in Peshawar tests four substances.
W: m.p. 660 °C; conducts as a solid and when molten; insoluble in water
X: m.p. 80 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water
Y: m.p. 770 °C; does not conduct as a solid; conducts when molten and when dissolved in water
Z: m.p. 3550 °C; does not conduct as a solid; insoluble in water

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the type of structure of each of W, X, Y and Z. Choose from: giant ionic, giant covalent, simple molecular, metallic.
parts.answer: W: metallic; X: simple molecular; Y: giant ionic; Z: giant covalent
parts.working: B1 each. W conducts as solid; X low m.p. and non-conductor; Y conducts only molten/dissolved; Z very high m.p., insoluble, non-conductor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Y conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid.
parts.answer: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice; in solution the ions are free to move and carry charge.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Silicon(IV) oxide melts at about 1700 °C but carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. Both are oxides of Group IV elements. Explain the difference in terms of structure and bonding.
parts.answer: SiO₂ is a giant covalent structure: melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds, needing a lot of energy. CO₂ is simple molecular: only weak intermolecular forces between molecules must be overcome.
parts.working: B1 SiO₂ giant covalent with many strong covalent bonds broken; B1 CO₂ simple molecules; B1 weak intermolecular forces need little energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Graphite and copper both conduct electricity. Compare how the charge is carried in each.
parts.answer: Both by delocalised electrons: in graphite each carbon atom has one delocalised electron, which moves along the layers; in copper the delocalised electrons move throughout the lattice of positive ions.
parts.working: B1 graphite: delocalised electrons (one per C, move along layers); B1 copper: sea of delocalised electrons around positive ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why magnesium oxide is used to line furnaces but sodium chloride is not.
parts.answer: MgO has a much higher melting point (stronger attraction between 2+ and 2− ions), so it does not melt at furnace temperatures.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why diamond is used in drill tips for cutting rock?
A Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid giant structure.
B Diamond has delocalised electrons between layers.
C Diamond is made of small molecules with strong bonds.
D Diamond has weak forces between layers.
parts.answer: A Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid giant structure.
parts.working: Four strong covalent bonds per atom in a 3-D giant lattice make diamond very hard. B and D describe graphite.

stem: Graphite is used as a dry lubricant in locks and as electrodes in electrolysis cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of graphite.
parts.answer: Layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons; each carbon is covalently bonded to three others; weak forces between the layers.
parts.working: B1 layers of hexagonal rings, each C bonded to 3 others; B1 weak forces between layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the structure to explain why graphite (i) is used as a lubricant (ii) is used for electrodes.
parts.answer: (i) The layers can slide over each other because forces between layers are weak. (ii) Each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move and carry charge.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂.
parts.answer: A giant covalent lattice in which each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms.
parts.working: B1 giant covalent / 3-D lattice; B1 each Si bonded to 4 O and each O to 2 Si.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to show that the formula is SiO₂.
parts.answer: Each Si has 4 bonds to O, but each O is shared between 2 Si, so each Si 'owns' 4 ÷ 2 = 2 O atoms; ratio Si : O = 1 : 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sand (mainly silicon(IV) oxide) is used to make glass. Explain why sand does not conduct electricity and has a high melting point.
parts.answer: No ions or delocalised electrons are free to move; many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it, needing much energy.
parts.working: B1 no mobile charged particles; B1 many strong covalent bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a mixture?
A air
B water
C sodium chloride
D copper
parts.answer: A air
parts.working: Air contains nitrogen, oxygen and other gases not chemically combined, in variable proportions. Water (B) is a compound with a fixed composition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the following as an element, a compound or a mixture: nitrogen, glucose, sea water, magnesium oxide, mercury, brass.
parts.answer: elements: nitrogen, mercury; compounds: glucose, magnesium oxide; mixtures: sea water, brass
parts.working: 3 marks for all six correct; 2 marks for 4–5; 1 mark for 2–3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two differences between a compound and a mixture.
parts.answer: A compound has a fixed composition and its elements are chemically bonded (can only be separated by chemical reactions); a mixture has variable composition, its components are not chemically bonded and can be separated by physical methods. A compound's properties differ from those of its elements.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: fixed vs variable composition; chemically combined vs not; separated by chemical vs physical means; properties of compound different from its elements.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a reaction pathway diagram the products are at a lower energy than the reactants. What does this show?
A The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.
B The reaction is endothermic and ΔH is positive.
C The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is positive.
D The reaction has no activation energy.
parts.answer: A The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.
parts.working: Energy is released to the surroundings, so products are lower and ΔH is negative. C has the wrong sign: exothermic means ΔH < 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A catalyst is added to a reaction. What happens to the activation energy and to the enthalpy change, ΔH?
A activation energy decreases; ΔH stays the same
B activation energy decreases; ΔH decreases
C activation energy increases; ΔH stays the same
D activation energy stays the same; ΔH decreases
parts.answer: A activation energy decreases; ΔH stays the same
parts.working: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy; the energies of reactants and products do not change, so ΔH is unchanged. B wrongly suggests the catalyst changes ΔH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by activation energy.
parts.answer: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The combustion of methane is exothermic. State whether ΔH is positive or negative and whether the products are above or below the reactants on its reaction pathway diagram.
parts.answer: ΔH is negative; the products are below the reactants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a gas cooker needs a spark or flame to light it, even though the reaction is exothermic.
parts.answer: The spark supplies the activation energy needed to start the reaction (after that, energy released keeps it going).

stem: On a reaction pathway diagram, the reactants are at 120 kJ/mol, the top of the energy 'hump' is at 310 kJ/mol and the products are at 40 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the forward reaction.
parts.answer: 190 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: ΔH = −80 kJ/mol; exothermic

author: HomiLabs

stem: For a thermal decomposition reaction, the reactants are at 0 kJ/mol, the top of the energy hump is at +250 kJ/mol and the products are at +90 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy and ΔH for the reaction without a catalyst.
parts.answer: activation energy 250 kJ/mol; ΔH = +90 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: With a catalyst the top of the hump is at +170 kJ/mol. Calculate the activation energy with the catalyst and state the value of ΔH with the catalyst.
parts.answer: 170 kJ/mol; ΔH = +90 kJ/mol (unchanged)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Give a reason.
parts.answer: Endothermic: the products have more energy than the reactants (ΔH positive).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can be kept at room temperature without reacting, but it explodes when a spark is applied. Explain this using the idea of activation energy.
parts.answer: At room temperature too few colliding molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the rate is negligible. The spark gives molecules enough energy to exceed the activation energy; the energy released then supplies other molecules.
parts.working: B1 particles at room temperature do not have energy ≥ Ea; B1 spark supplies the activation energy (then the reaction sustains itself).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O and it is strongly exothermic. Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. Say where reactants and products are and how ΔH and the activation energy are shown.
parts.answer: Reactants (2H₂ + O₂) on the left at a higher level; a curve rising to a peak then falling to products (2H₂O) at a lower level. Activation energy: arrow from reactants up to the peak. ΔH: arrow from reactants down to products (negative).
parts.working: B1 products below reactants; B1 Ea from reactant level to top of curve; B1 ΔH arrow from reactants down to products.

stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. ΔH = −98 kJ per mole of H₂O₂. The activation energy is 75 kJ/mol without a catalyst and 58 kJ/mol with manganese(IV) oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in activation energy caused by the catalyst.
parts.answer: 17 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of ΔH for the catalysed reaction.
parts.answer: −98 kJ/mol
parts.working: B1 a catalyst does not change ΔH.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles and energy, why the catalysed reaction is faster.
parts.answer: With a lower activation energy, a larger fraction of colliding particles have energy equal to or above the activation energy, so there are more successful collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 more particles have energy ≥ Ea; B1 more successful collisions per unit time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lime kilns near Rohri in Sindh heat limestone to make quicklime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calcium carbonate is decomposed in a lime kiln: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, ΔH = +178 kJ/mol. Describe the reaction pathway diagram you would draw for this reaction, including how each label is placed.
parts.answer: Energy axis upward; reactant level CaCO₃ lower, product level CaO + CO₂ higher; curve from reactants rising to a peak above the product level, then down to products; activation energy shown by an arrow from reactants to the peak; ΔH (+178 kJ/mol) shown by an upward arrow from reactants to products.
parts.working: B1 products higher than reactants; B1 curve with a peak above both levels; B1 Ea arrow reactants → peak; B1 ΔH arrow reactants → products, labelled positive / +178.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the kiln must be heated strongly all the time, not just to start the reaction.
parts.answer: The reaction is endothermic: it takes in energy continuously, so heat must be supplied throughout.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A reversible reaction has a forward activation energy of 160 kJ/mol and ΔH = −45 kJ/mol for the forward reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy for the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: 205 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 the peak is 160 kJ/mol above reactants and products are 45 kJ/mol below reactants; A1 160 + 45 = 205.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State ΔH for the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: +45 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy to 110 kJ/mol. Calculate the new activation energy for the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: 155 kJ/mol
parts.working: B1 110 + 45 = 155 (a catalyst lowers both by the same amount).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The energy profile of a reaction shows: reactants at 50 kJ/mol, the peak at 300 kJ/mol and products at 230 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the forward reaction.
parts.answer: +180 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the forward reaction and of the reverse reaction.
parts.answer: forward 250 kJ/mol; reverse 70 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: In this reaction, is more energy taken in when bonds break or given out when bonds form? Explain.
parts.answer: More energy is taken in to break bonds than is released when new bonds form, because ΔH is positive (endothermic).
parts.working: B1 bond breaking > bond making; B1 linked to positive ΔH / endothermic.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Data for two reactions:
Reaction A: activation energy 30 kJ/mol, ΔH = −20 kJ/mol
Reaction B: activation energy 180 kJ/mol, ΔH = −400 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which reaction would you expect to be faster at room temperature? Explain.
parts.answer: Reaction A: its activation energy (30 kJ/mol) is much lower, so many more colliding particles have enough energy to react.
parts.working: B1 A; B1 lower Ea → greater proportion of collisions successful.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which reaction releases more energy per mole? Calculate how many times more.
parts.answer: Reaction B; 20 times more

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says: 'Reaction B has a very negative ΔH, so it must be very fast.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: The statement is wrong. ΔH only tells how much energy is released overall; rate depends on the activation energy. B has a high activation energy, so it is slow at room temperature even though it is very exothermic.
parts.working: B1 ΔH does not determine rate; B1 rate depends on Ea, which is high for B.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process is endothermic?
A burning petrol in a car engine
B dissolving ammonium nitrate in water
C adding dilute hydrochloric acid to sodium hydroxide solution
D the rusting of iron
parts.answer: B dissolving ammonium nitrate in water
parts.working: Dissolving ammonium nitrate takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls (used in cold packs). Neutralisation (C) gives out heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an exothermic reaction and by an endothermic reaction.
parts.answer: Exothermic: transfers thermal energy to the surroundings (temperature of surroundings rises). Endothermic: takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (temperature falls).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Classify each process as exothermic or endothermic:
(i) burning natural gas in a stove
(ii) photosynthesis in leaves
(iii) thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
(iv) magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid
parts.answer: (i) exothermic (ii) endothermic (iii) endothermic (iv) exothermic

stem:
A student mixes 25 cm³ of four different pairs of solutions, A–D, in a polystyrene cup and records the temperatures.
reaction: initial temperature / final temperature (°C)
A: 22.0 / 31.5
B: 22.5 / 16.0
C: 21.0 / 21.5
D: 23.0 / 35.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature change for each reaction. Use + for a rise and − for a fall.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which reaction is endothermic? Give a reason.
parts.answer: B, because the temperature fell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which reaction is the most exothermic? Give a reason.
parts.answer: D, because it has the largest temperature rise.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student used the same volume of solution each time.
parts.answer: To make it a fair test: the same volume means temperature changes can be compared.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cold pack for sports injuries contains solid ammonium nitrate and a separate bag of water. When the pack is squeezed the solid dissolves and the pack gets cold. Explain why it gets cold.
parts.answer: Dissolving ammonium nitrate is endothermic; it takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (the pack and the skin), so the temperature falls.
parts.working: B1 endothermic; B1 energy taken in from surroundings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A self-heating hand warmer works by the slow oxidation of iron powder. State whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic and state the sign of ΔH.
parts.answer: Exothermic; ΔH is negative.

stem:
A student adds aqueous sodium hydroxide, 5 cm³ at a time, to 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup with a lid and records the highest temperature after each addition.
volume of NaOH added / cm³: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35
temperature / °C: 24.0, 27.1, 30.0, 32.8, 35.2, 35.0, 34.1, 33.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum temperature rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to estimate the volume of sodium hydroxide that exactly neutralises the acid.
parts.answer: about 20 cm³ (where the temperature is highest)
parts.working: B1 20 cm³ (accept 20–22 cm³ from the highest temperature).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature falls after 20 cm³ of alkali has been added.
parts.answer: The acid has all reacted, so no more heat is released; adding more (cooler) alkali cools the mixture, and heat is lost to the surroundings.
parts.working: B1 reaction complete / no more energy released; B1 cooler solution added / heat loss.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a polystyrene cup with a lid is used rather than a glass beaker.
parts.answer: Polystyrene is a good insulator and the lid reduces heat loss, so the temperature rise measured is more accurate.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether bond breaking and bond making are exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: Bond breaking is endothermic; bond making is exothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The burning of hydrogen is exothermic. Explain this in terms of the energy changes when bonds are broken and made.
parts.answer: The energy released when the new O–H bonds form is greater than the energy taken in to break the H–H and O=O bonds.
parts.working: B1 energy released forming bonds; B1 greater than energy absorbed breaking bonds.

stem:
A student adds 1.0 g of a powdered metal to 25 cm³ of aqueous copper(II) sulfate in an insulated cup. The starting temperature is 20.0 °C each time.
metal: highest temperature / °C
magnesium: 58.5
zinc: 31.0
iron: 26.5
silver: 20.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise for each metal.
parts.answer: magnesium 38.5 °C; zinc 11.0 °C; iron 6.5 °C; silver 0.0 °C
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to put the four metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.answer: magnesium > zinc > iron > silver

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there was no temperature change with silver.
parts.answer: Silver is less reactive than copper, so it does not displace copper and no reaction occurs.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one variable, other than the volume of solution, that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: Mass of metal / particle size (powder) / concentration of copper(II) sulfate / starting temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student dissolves 5.0 g of potassium nitrate in 50 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature falls from 21.5 °C to 15.3 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature change with 5.0 g of potassium nitrate.
parts.answer: −6.2 °C (a fall of 6.2 °C)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the temperature change is proportional to the mass dissolved in the same volume of water, predict the final temperature when 10.0 g is dissolved, starting at 21.5 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In practice the measured fall with 10.0 g was smaller than predicted. Suggest one reason.
parts.answer: Heat is absorbed from the surroundings during the experiment (more time to dissolve), or not all the solid dissolved.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student compares two liquid fuels by heating 200 cm³ of water in a copper can with a spirit burner.
fuel: mass burned / g, temperature rise / °C
X: 0.92, 18.4
Y: 1.25, 30.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise per gram of fuel burned for each fuel.
parts.answer: fuel X: 20.0 °C per g; fuel Y: 24.0 °C per g
parts.working: M1 rise ÷ mass; A1 both values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which fuel releases more energy per gram? Explain.
parts.answer: Fuel Y, because it gives the larger temperature rise per gram for the same mass of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why the results are lower than the true values, and suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the air and to the can; incomplete combustion (soot on the can); some heat warms the can not the water. Improvement: shield the flame from draughts / put a lid on the can / keep the flame close to the can.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sources of error; 1 mark for a matching improvement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complete combustion of methane has ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. Calculate the energy released when 4.0 g of methane is burned. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: 2NH₃ → N₂ + 3H₂, ΔH = +92 kJ (for 2 mol of ammonia). Calculate the energy needed to decompose 3.4 g of ammonia. (Ar: N = 14, H = 1)
parts.answer: 9.2 kJ
parts.working: M1 Mr NH₃ = 17, moles = 0.20; M1 energy per mol NH₃ = 46 kJ; A1 0.20 × 46 = 9.2 kJ.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431.
What is the enthalpy change for this reaction?
A −184 kJ/mol
B +184 kJ/mol
C +247 kJ/mol
D −862 kJ/mol
parts.answer: A −184 kJ/mol
parts.working: Bonds broken 436 + 242 = 678; bonds made 2 × 431 = 862; ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. B has the wrong sign (made − broken); C uses only one H–Cl bond.

stem:
H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
parts.answer: 629 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when the bonds in the products form.
parts.answer: 732 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: −103 kJ/mol; exothermic

author: HomiLabs

stem:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy released when the bonds in the products form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane.
parts.answer: −818 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ammonia is made by the Haber process, for example at the fertiliser plants in Pakistan.
Bond energies in kJ/mol: N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
parts.answer: −93 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy change when 1 mole of ammonia is formed.
parts.answer: −46.5 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: C=C 612, C–C 347, C–H 413, H–H 436

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the reaction C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆, which bonds are broken and which bonds are made? (You may ignore bonds that are present on both sides.)
parts.answer: Broken: C=C and H–H. Made: C–C and two C–H bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the reaction.
parts.answer: −125 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, O=O 498, O–H 464

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
parts.answer: −486 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per mole of hydrogen burned.
parts.answer: 243 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hydrogen is used as a fuel in some buses. Give one advantage of hydrogen as a fuel.
parts.answer: The only product is water (no carbon dioxide).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
H₂ + F₂ → 2HF   ΔH = −542 kJ/mol
Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, H–F 568

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bond energy of the F–F bond.
parts.answer: 158 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why fluorine is very reactive.
parts.answer: The F–F bond is weak (needs little energy to break), and strong bonds form in the products.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: C–H 413, C–C 347, C–O 358, O–H 464, O=O 498, C=O 805

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the bonds broken in one molecule of ethanol, C₂H₅OH.
parts.answer: 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O, 1 O–H
parts.working: B1 all four types with correct numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the complete combustion of ethanol: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
parts.answer: −1276 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: The data-book value is −1367 kJ/mol. Suggest why the value calculated from bond energies is different.
parts.answer: Bond energies are average values from many compounds (and the data assume all substances are gases).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: O–H 464, O–O 146, O=O 498

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Each H₂O₂ molecule has the structure H–O–O–H. Calculate ΔH for the equation as written.
parts.answer: −206 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that, in this reaction, the only bonds that really change are two O–O single bonds broken and one O=O double bond made, and that this gives the same answer.
parts.answer: The four O–H bonds are present on both sides and cancel. ΔH = 2 × 146 − 498 = −206 kJ/mol.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which metal is extracted from its oxide by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon?
A aluminium
B iron
C zinc
D copper
parts.answer: A aluminium
parts.working: Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide. Iron (B) is below carbon and is extracted with carbon (as carbon monoxide) in the blast furnace.

stem: Iron is made in a blast furnace from hematite, coke, limestone and hot air.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each raw material:
(i) coke
(ii) limestone
(iii) hot air
parts.answer: (i) burns to provide heat and forms carbon monoxide, the reducing agent (ii) removes acidic impurities such as silicon(IV) oxide, forming slag (iii) provides oxygen for the coke to burn

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the main ore of iron used.
parts.answer: hematite (iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations for: (i) the formation of carbon monoxide from coke in two steps (ii) the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide.
parts.answer: (i) C + O₂ → CO₂ then CO₂ + C → 2CO (ii) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
parts.working: B1 C + O₂ → CO₂; B1 CO₂ + C → 2CO; B1 balanced reduction equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the reaction in (a)(ii), name the substance that is reduced and the reducing agent.
parts.answer: iron(III) oxide is reduced; carbon monoxide is the reducing agent

parts.label: a
parts.text: Limestone decomposes in the furnace. Write the equation.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium oxide reacts with silicon(IV) oxide (sand) to form slag. Write the equation and name the slag.
parts.answer: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃; calcium silicate

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain this reaction in terms of the types of oxide involved.
parts.answer: Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and silicon(IV) oxide is an acidic oxide, so they react (neutralise) to form a salt.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how the slag and the molten iron are removed separately.
parts.answer: Slag is less dense, so it floats on the molten iron and is tapped off at a higher level.

stem: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide (from bauxite) dissolved in molten cryolite, using carbon electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite rather than melted on its own.
parts.answer: Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000 °C); the solution in molten cryolite works at a much lower temperature (about 950 °C), saving energy and cost.
parts.working: B1 lowers the operating temperature; B1 saves energy / cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equations for the reactions at the cathode and at the anode.
parts.answer: cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon anodes must be replaced regularly.
parts.answer: The oxygen produced at the hot anodes reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away.
parts.working: B1 oxygen reacts with carbon; B1 forms CO₂ / anodes wear away.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict which of these oxides can be reduced by heating with carbon: magnesium oxide, zinc oxide, copper(II) oxide, aluminium oxide. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: zinc oxide and copper(II) oxide; zinc and copper are less reactive than carbon, so carbon can remove the oxygen. Magnesium and aluminium are more reactive than carbon.
parts.working: B1 zinc oxide; B1 copper(II) oxide (and no others); B1 reason based on position relative to carbon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student heats black copper(II) oxide with carbon powder in a crucible. Write the balanced equation and state what is seen at the end.
parts.answer: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂; pink-brown (orange-brown) solid copper forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of iron that can be obtained from 800 tonnes of iron(III) oxide. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
parts.answer: 560 tonnes
parts.working: M1 Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160 and 112 t Fe in every 160 t; A1 800 × 112 ÷ 160 = 560 t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of hematite ore is 90 % iron(III) oxide by mass. Calculate the maximum mass of iron from 1000 tonnes of this ore.
parts.answer: 630 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the actual mass of iron produced is less than this.
parts.answer: Not all the iron oxide is reduced / some iron is lost in the slag.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The overall reaction is 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Calculate the mass of aluminium produced from 51 tonnes of aluminium oxide. (Ar: Al = 27, O = 16)
parts.answer: 27 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen produced at the same time.
parts.answer: 24 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why recycling aluminium cans is better than extracting new aluminium.
parts.answer: Recycling uses much less electrical energy; it conserves bauxite ore; it reduces waste in landfill; less mining and land damage.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copper is used for electrical wiring in houses. Which two properties make it suitable?
A good electrical conductor and ductile
B high density and brittle
C low melting point and hard
D reacts with water and conducts heat
parts.answer: A good electrical conductor and ductile
parts.working: Wiring needs a metal that conducts electricity well and can be drawn into wires (ductile). B is wrong: copper is not brittle, and density is not the reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three physical properties that are typical of metals.
parts.answer: Any three of: good conductors of electricity; good conductors of heat; malleable; ductile; shiny when freshly cut; high melting and boiling points; high density; sonorous.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one chemical property that is typical of metals.
parts.answer: Metals form basic oxides / form positive ions / reactive metals produce hydrogen with dilute acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aluminium is used for overhead power cables. Give two properties.
parts.answer: Good electrical conductor; low density (light, so pylons can support it); resistant to corrosion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why aluminium is used to make aircraft bodies.
parts.answer: Low density (strong but light, especially as an alloy) and resistant to corrosion because of its oxide layer.
parts.working: B1 low density; B1 corrosion resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why copper is used for water pipes.
parts.answer: It does not react with water / is unreactive and does not corrode easily; it is easy to bend (malleable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid, and give one observation.
parts.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; effervescence (bubbles) / magnesium disappears / mixture gets warm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calcium reacts with cold water. Write the balanced equation and describe a test for the gas produced.
parts.answer: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂; a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
parts.working: B1 formulae; B1 balanced; B1 test and result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is seen when copper is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, and explain.
parts.answer: No reaction (no bubbles), because copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

stem:
Data for four metals:
metal: density / g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity, cost, resistance to corrosion
W: 2.7, 61, low, good
X: 8.9, 100, high, good
Y: 7.9, 17, low, poor
Z: 19.3, 73, very high, excellent

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which metal is best for overhead power cables? Use the data to explain.
parts.answer: W: low density with good conductivity, low cost and good corrosion resistance.
parts.working: B1 W; B1 two supporting data points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative conductivity divided by density for W and for X. Give your answers to 3 significant figures and explain what they show.
parts.answer: W: 22.6; X: 11.2. W conducts about twice as well as X for the same mass of cable.
parts.working: M1 61 ÷ 2.7; A1 22.6 and 11.2; B1 W better per unit mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why Y is not used for a bridge near the sea in Gwadar unless it is protected.
parts.answer: Y has poor corrosion resistance; it would corrode (rust) quickly in moist, salty air.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series but aluminium cooking pots do not react with water. Explain why.
parts.answer: Aluminium is covered by a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide that sticks to the surface and stops water reaching the metal.
parts.working: B1 oxide layer; B1 layer protects / prevents further reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A piece of aluminium foil is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. At first nothing happens; after a few minutes bubbles appear quickly. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: The acid first reacts with / removes the oxide layer (no gas). Once the metal is exposed, the reactive aluminium reacts with the acid, giving hydrogen.
parts.working: B1 oxide layer removed by acid first; B1 then Al reacts producing hydrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture reacts?
A copper and aqueous zinc sulfate
B iron and aqueous copper(II) sulfate
C silver and aqueous iron(II) sulfate
D copper and aqueous magnesium chloride
parts.answer: B iron and aqueous copper(II) sulfate
parts.working: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from solution. In A, copper is less reactive than zinc, so there is no reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of magnesium ribbon is placed in blue aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Give two observations.
parts.answer: The blue colour fades; a pink-brown solid (copper) forms on the magnesium; the solution gets warm; the magnesium gets smaller.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation and the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu; Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is called a displacement reaction.
parts.answer: The more reactive magnesium takes the place of (displaces) the less reactive copper from its compound.

stem:
A student places small pieces of metals P, Q and R in solutions of their nitrates and records whether a reaction happens (✓) or not (✗).
P in Q nitrate: ✓   P in R nitrate: ✓
Q in P nitrate: ✗   Q in R nitrate: ✓
R in P nitrate: ✗   R in Q nitrate: ✗

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the metals P, Q and R in order of reactivity, most reactive first. Explain how you decided.
parts.answer: P > Q > R. P displaces both Q and R; Q displaces only R; R displaces neither.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether R would react with dilute hydrochloric acid if R is copper. Explain.
parts.answer: No; copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one safety precaution and one way to make the comparison fair.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection; use the same size / mass of each metal and the same volume and concentration of solution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how potassium, calcium and copper react (if at all) with cold water.
parts.answer: Potassium: reacts violently, melts, moves around and the hydrogen burns with a lilac flame. Calcium: reacts steadily with bubbling, forming a cloudy solution. Copper: no reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but reacts with steam. Write the equation for the reaction with steam.
parts.answer: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the order of reactivity in terms of the tendency to form positive ions.
parts.answer: The more reactive the metal, the more easily its atoms lose electrons to form positive ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The thermite reaction is used to weld railway lines: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. Explain why this reaction happens.
parts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
parts.answer: oxidising agent: iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃); reducing agent: aluminium

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron formed from 5.4 g of aluminium. (Ar: Al = 27, Fe = 56)

stem:
A metal M is tested.
M in aqueous zinc sulfate: no change
M in aqueous copper(II) sulfate: brown coating forms, solution fades
M in dilute sulfuric acid: slow bubbling

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to place M in the reactivity series relative to zinc, copper and hydrogen.
parts.answer: Below zinc, above copper and above hydrogen.
parts.working: B1 between zinc and copper; B1 above hydrogen (reacts with acid).

parts.label: b
